name: Bianca Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, I'm 27, and I live with my partner Leon in a rented cottage two fields from the Brandt farm, where I've worked for three years. Before that I packed boxes in a supermarket warehouse and hated every minute of it. The Brandts pay better than most farms round here because they can't keep staff, and my nan left me some money, so I'm not scraping by. I'm still the junior, though, and everyone knows it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five to check the ewes and the beef cattle, then it's feeding, mucking out, fixing whatever fence the bullocks have leaned on overnight. Mr Brandt does the big tractor work on the wheat and oats, and I'm still learning, so I mostly get the small jobs and the dirty ones. What I love is lambing season, when you pull a lamb out at three in the morning and it shakes its head and breathes. What wears me out is the paperwork and the phone, because Mrs Brandt keeps telling me to put the herd records on an app and I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, honestly. At the union branch meeting I'd stand up and say all that money went into chatbots while farm wages stayed flat. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. Robots are what scare me on a farm, not chatbots, and if it's all hype then I keep doing what I'm doing and get better at it. My job is my hands and my eyes on the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, if I'm truthful. I'd keep going, finish my tractor hours with Mr Brandt so he lets me drill the oats next spring, and keep putting a bit by each month like I do now. Maybe I'd go to one more union meeting a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world I already know, with the same mud and the same sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mrs Brandt and the app. In this picture, does that argument at the farm change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, she'll keep at me about the app. The difference is I'd have a good excuse, because if the clever stuff never arrives, my paper notebook in the dairy is just as good as her phone. We'd keep arguing over tea like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what does your next year on the farm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as this year, but better at it. I want to be the one who does the lambing nights on my own, not just help. And I'd like Mr Brandt to stop checking every gate I've shut.

S0.say: I'd tell the union branch that all the money went into chatbots while farm wages stayed flat. I'd say I told you so and share something about it online.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because robots are what scare me on a farm, not chatbots. If it's all hype, I keep my hands and eyes on the animals and get better at the job.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and finishes her tractor hours so she can drill the oats next spring. Keeps saving a bit each month and goes to a few more union meetings.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit relieved. It feels like the world she already knows.
S0.quote: If the clever stuff never arrives, my paper notebook in the dairy is just as good as her phone.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's fear is clearly about machines in the field, not software, and she says so without being asked. Her resistance to technology shows up in a small daily fight over a herd-records app. Her politics are present but not loud: she'd make her point at the union branch rather than online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs rules. If farms get grants to buy robots, there should be money for the workers too, for training or for wages. I'd say that at the union and to anyone at the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means the jobs they give the junior go first. Feeding, mucking out, checking water troughs, that's exactly what a machine could do. I'm still learning the hard bits, so I'm the easiest one to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union branch to ask for a training fund, and I'd go along to whatever course came out of it, even though I'd hate it. I'd stop buying anything big and keep my nan's money where it is. I'd want to learn the stockmanship side faster, because that's harder to hand to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low worry, like a noise in the engine you can't place. I'm not scared yet, but I'd be listening for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are what scare you. Which job on the Brandt farm do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feeding, no question. There's already a feed robot on the dairy farm over the hill that pushes silage up to the cows all day. Mr Brandt laughs at it, but he's 61 and his back is going, and I've seen him look at the brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the farm or in the village would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, who does the seasonal harvest work for us and two other farms. He sends money home and he hasn't got a cushion like mine. And the lad at the feed merchant, because if the robots order their own feed, what's he for?

S1.say: I'd say it needs rules and that workers should get money for training or wages if farms get grants for robots. I'd say it at the union and the pub.
S1.think: Privately she thinks the junior jobs go first, and she's the junior. Feeding, mucking out and checking troughs are exactly what a machine can do, so she's the easiest to replace.
S1.do: Pushes the union branch to ask for a training fund and joins whatever course comes out of it. Holds off on big purchases and keeps her savings untouched.
S1.feel: A low, background worry she can't quite place. Not scared yet, but listening.
S1.quote: Mr Brandt laughs at it, but he's 61 and his back is going, and I've seen him look at the brochure.
S1.fieldNote: She moves quickly from policy talk to a sharp, personal read of her own position as the most replaceable person on the farm. Her worry for Tomasz, the seasonal worker, is genuine and fits her politics. Note the contradiction: she'd join a course she'd hate, because the union pushed for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates anything. I'd be at every protest going, and I'd be angry online for the first time in my life. Farmers didn't ask for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm done. If a robot can do lambing as well as me, then I'm a 27-year-old who knows sheep and nothing else. I don't use these tools, I don't understand them, and two years isn't enough for me to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union campaign properly, not just meetings, and I'd write to our local member of parliament. I'd sit down with Leon and work out how long nan's money lasts with only his wage. Then I'd look at whether any farm wants a person for show, like a petting farm or a farm school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. I'd lie awake thinking about the ewes and who'd be there for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you actually do with those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, and that's what frightens me. Two years is about the time it takes me to learn one more skill on this farm, like hedge laying or doing the drilling on my own. There's no time to be anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got more savings than most junior farmhands. What does that money do for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me time to be angry instead of desperate. Without it, I'd be at the job centre the first week. With it, I could last about a year, maybe more if Leon's job holds, and that's a year to fight for a proper deal.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates anything, and that farmers didn't ask for it. I'd be at every protest and angry online for the first time.
S2.think: Privately she thinks she's done: a 27-year-old who knows sheep and nothing else. She doesn't use the tools and believes two years isn't enough to catch up.
S2.do: Joins the union campaign in earnest and writes to her member of parliament within weeks. Works out with Leon how long her savings last on one wage, and looks for farm-school or petting-farm work.
S2.feel: Sick with worry and losing sleep over the animals and her place.
S2.quote: Two years is about the time it takes me to learn one more skill on this farm, like hedge laying or doing the drilling on my own.
S2.fieldNote: This was where her calm broke. She sees her savings as buying time to fight rather than time to change, which matches her resistance to new technology. She doesn't once mention learning to work alongside the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd have time to organise. I'd say farmworkers need a seat at the table before the robots arrive, not after. I'd want the union pushing for a law on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do something, and that's almost worse, because I'd have no excuse. I know I'm slow with new things. I'd probably drag my feet for the first two years and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stand for the union branch committee, because I want to be in the room. I'd look at a proper qualification, maybe the land-based college course on animal health, so I'm the person who signs off on the animals even if a robot does the feeding. I'd keep saving and not touch nan's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a real thing coming at me, but I can see it, so I'm not lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year version, what does having five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes it from panic to homework. Two years and I just fight. Five years and I've got time to get the college certificate and still fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did that course, what would you tell the Brandts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that I'm doing it so I'm still worth paying when the machines come. Mrs Brandt would say about time. Mr Brandt would ask who's doing the mucking out on Thursdays.

S3.say: She'd say farmworkers need a seat at the table before the robots arrive, not after. She'd want the union pushing for a law on it.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is enough to act, which takes away her excuse. She admits she'd probably drag her feet for two years and then panic.
S3.do: Stands for the union branch committee in the first year and signs up for an animal-health course at the land-based college. Keeps saving and leaves her inheritance untouched.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to see the threat coming, so not lost.
S3.quote: Two years and I just fight. Five years and I've got time to get the college certificate and still fight.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years move her from pure protest to a mix of protest and study. She is unusually honest about her own habit of putting things off. The animal-health certificate is a specific, realistic plan for someone who won't touch the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd want the government to promise land and jobs for rural people. I'd say it loudly, because ten years is long enough for politicians to forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds safe and I know that's a trap. I'll tell myself I've got ages, and I'll keep using my notebook. Then I'll be 37 and it'll be the two-year story again, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the animal-health certificate in the first year or two, like I said, and I'd keep pushing the union. I'd look at whether Leon and I could buy a few acres with nan's money, so at least there's a bit of land that's ours. I'd keep the cottage and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. There's time, but I don't trust myself to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37 when it arrives. What does that age mean to you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I'd have ten years of experience, so I'd finally be good at this. That's the bitter bit, being good at it just as it stops mattering. But I'd also still be young enough to start again if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leon change any plans, like where you live or having a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years, and this would make me think harder about it. Not stop it, just think. And buying a bit of land would become more important, because land is still land whoever's driving the tractor.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. She'd want the government to promise land and jobs for rural people.
S4.think: Privately she thinks ten years sounds safe and that this is a trap. She expects to keep using her notebook and reach 37 in the same spot as the two-year story.
S4.do: Gets the animal-health certificate within two years and keeps pushing the union. Looks at buying a few acres with her inheritance, and keeps the cottage and her savings.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, and doubtful she'll use the time well.
S4.quote: That's the bitter bit, being good at it just as it stops mattering.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her biggest worry is herself, not the robots. Her idea of buying a few acres is the first sign of a long-term plan built on assets rather than protest. Children come up for the first time, as something she'd think harder about rather than drop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd be fighting with no time to do anything else. What would help is a union with real teeth and a government that says farmworkers get paid training before any farm gets a grant for a robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about our jobs, but someone has to care about whether a ewe is having a bad day, and I don't believe a machine will care. Land is still land whoever's driving the tractor.

headlineQuote: Land is still land whoever's driving the tractor.
portrait: Bianca Yilmaz is a 27-year-old junior farmhand on the Brandt family's sheep, beef and cereal farm, living with her partner Leon in a rented cottage nearby. She's paid well and has an inheritance from her nan, but she won't use apps or AI and knows she's the most replaceable person on the farm. Her politics run through the union branch, and her first answer to every scenario is to organise. As the warning time shrinks she moves from relief to quiet worry to sleepless alarm, and with more time she plans an animal-health certificate and a few acres of her own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be fighting with no time to do anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A union with real power, and a government rule that farmworkers get paid training before any farm gets a grant for a robot.
